items.title: FFXIV Online Store Selling Modern Aesthetics Hair Cuts Separately
items.summary: It is possible to get FFXIV Online Store Modern Aesthetics hairstyles alone instead of hair cuts only being sold with costumes.
items.content:
Square Enix took to social media to reveal a change to the way the Final Fantasy XIV Online Store works that makes it possible to buy the FFXIV Modern Aesthetics hair cuts from certain glamour attire instead of being forced to buy a whole costume with outfit to unlock additional hairstyles. 14 are available via this method on the online store as of time of writing. In each case, it costs $5 for the hairstyle alone.

Here’s the full list of the now sold separately Modern Aesthetics FFXIV hair cuts available as individual hairstyles in the Final Fantasy XIV Online Store. In the case of the ones that previously appeared in the FFXIII Lightning’s Attire and Snow’s Attire costume sets, the two are being sold together for $5 here as Modern Aesthetics – Pulse. However, the female and male versions of the Omega hairstyle are sold separately.

The outfits for each of the characters above when sold alone are $12 each. If someone wants the costume and Modern Aesthetics hairstyles, then it tends to cost $15 for the bundles.

Final Fantasy XIV is available for the Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC, and the FFXIV Evercold expansion is set to appear in January 2027.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV Online (Switch 2) - An Expansive Port That Demands Your Commitment
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV Online has been through quite a rollercoaster journey over the years on its way to becoming one of the most respected MMOs in the industry. Its 2010 launch was a disaster, plagued with performance issues and shoddy design that torpedoed its reputation.

Rather than pulling the plug early, Square decided to swap in a new director to salvage it, leading to a reboot in 2013 called A Realm Reborn. Since then, the game has mostly gone from strength to strength across over a decade of expansions and is now in the process of building up its second major arc.

Though this isn’t the first time Square Enix has brought Final Fantasy XIV to console, it is the first time it’s come to a Nintendo platform, and I’m happy to report that it stuck the landing. The full fat experience is here in all its glory, giving you access to a high quality and addictive RPG experience that’s sure to be in the running for one of the most content-rich games ever produced for a handheld.

The narrative places you in the role of a self-insert character in the land of Eorzea who comes into the picture just as geopolitical tensions are on the rise. After a catastrophic war five years earlier, the expansionist Garlean Empire was repelled by the city-states comprising the Eorzean Alliance, but its leaders desire revenge and are winding up for another grab at ultimate control.

Amid this, you’re also told through a vision by a mysterious goddess of light named Hydaelyn that you’re her chosen champion, and she tasks you with finding six magical crystals to ward off the servants of an approaching darkness.

Thus, we set off on the early steps of what came to be called the Hydaelyn-Zodiark Saga, a four-part fantasy epic that should take you no less than two-hundred hours to complete, and that’s assuming that you beeline for the finale and engage in almost no side content. After all that, there’s then a whole other expansion that’s in the early stages of setting up the next ten-year arc.

Suffice to say, Final Fantasy XIV features one of the richest storylines available in a modern RPG, weaving together the subplots of various nations, factions, and supporting characters to make for an impressively complex and deep narrative.

The downside to this, however, is that the pacing can be all over the place. The 60-hour story of the base game alone is basically an extended exposition dump detailing all the major players in the world and setting the stage for the building conflict to come, meaning you spend a lot of time scrolling through line after line of unvoiced text from NPCs telling you about very interesting story beats that happened some other time offscreen.

This leads to a narrative experience with some incredible highs and disappointing lows. Once the plot picks up steam and starts focusing more on current events, there are lots of awesome character moments and payoffs that make all the time investment up to that point feel worth it. Yet between those moments, it can sometimes feel like the plot really takes its time focusing on largely irrelevant or uninteresting subjects that you simply have to endure to reach the good stuff.

Gameplay design follows the expected structure of an MMO, giving you an enormous living world to explore packed with jobs and levels to grind, side quests to fulfill, minigames to fool around with, dungeons to raid, and a massive story to gradually uncover.

As long as you stick to the Main Story Quest chain, you'll be toured around all the main points of interest in an area and progressively introduced to core mechanics and objectives at a measured pace. Side quest content then fills out the world with more detail and texture, though tons of the quest objectives admittedly boil down to 'bring me three boar skins' fetch quests.

A big part of what makes the gameplay loop so addicting is the versatility of your character, who can independently level dozens of jobs that fill out various combat and non-combat roles. In a combat role, your job is built around a growing variety of cooldown-based actions, echoing the classic Final Fantasy ATB system that blends turn-based and action gameplay.

Every combat job has its own distinct gimmicks and features, such as how the Thaumaturge operates by repeatedly shifting between two passive states that bolster either damage output or MP regeneration. Mechanics like this keep fights from feeling too much like you’re just watching cooldown icons on a hotbar, and there are enough distinguishing traits to make the various classes all feel like they’re worth experimenting with.

Non-combat roles are just as dynamic, even without the pressure of attacking foes. If you're working as a Goldsmith, you can create various bits of armour and jewellery, and it's much more involved than merely clicking the 'Craft' button on a menu after you have the materials.

items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Sets a Higher Bar for HD-2D and Brings the RPG Series Back to Turn-Based
items.summary: Final Fantasy Resonance retools Brave Exvius and sets a new benchmark for HD-2D visuals alongside solid turn-based combat and incredible music, which carry an underwhelming story.
items.content:
To evoke the classics is also to hold yourself to the high standard set by them. With Final Fantasy Resonance bringing the venerated series back to its origins with turn-based combat, and wielding Square’s HD-2D art style to modernize nostalgia for the pixel art era, it plucks at something I've longed for as someone who grew up in the SNES generation. While I've expressed my love for the Octopath Traveler series time and again, Final Fantasy has of course crystalized into something meaningful over the past several decades. But as much as Resonance looks like a torchbearer for classic RPGs, it also goes for a style of storytelling that often rings hollow. So, I think of it as a game of moments – when a genre-fusing boss theme graces your ears, when you execute a turn perfectly and watch all your spells fire off with big damage numbers, and when a cutscene brings HD-2D to life in a way you've just never seen before.

Resonance adapts the story and characters from the now-shuttered mobile game Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius by packaging them into the structure of a traditional RPG; no gacha mechanics, no microtransactions. It's quite similar to what Square Enix did with Octopath Traveler 0 and it's a brilliant way to bring existing stories into a format I'm a lot more inclined to play. With that comes an overworld with towns to represent each region, random encounters, an airship for roaming free and discovering pieces of land that feel like secrets, and full voice acting throughout the main story.

It largely sticks to the events of the first season of Brave Exvius, which follows the knights from the Kingdom of Grandshelt, Rain and Laswell, the mysterious magical girl born from a crystal, Fina, along with additional friends on a quest to stop the armor-clad Sworn Six from destroying the world's crystals and plunging it into calamity. Of course, there's more beneath the surface. That said, a lot of dialogue and interstitial events have been added to fill out the journey, which took me about 45 hours to complete (including all of the side quests marked on my map and poking around the overworld for optional minibosses who offer intense challenges). While chunks of Resonance's story aren't very riveting, the production value here had me forgetting that this was built on the bones of a mobile game – not that Brave Exvius was any lesser of an achievement for what it was.

That retooling extends to gameplay, which retains concepts and mechanics that work extremely well as an engaging turn-based combat system – and hearing "turn-based" and Final Fantasy in the same breath after all these years released those good chemicals in my brain, too. This is not an ATB system with an active element, but a straightforward turn order along a timeline. And the way you either plan accordingly depending on which units are up or manipulate the order to your advantage had me employing similar strategies as I do in the Trails series or the Octopath Traveler games.

It's all about elemental affinities and staggering enemies in Resonance, however. Each party member has their own set of elements covered through magic spells or element-imbued physical attacks, but they also equip what are called Visions that function somewhat like a Job system directly inspired by Final Fantasy V. This is what provides flexibility in party composition, giving you the tools to make sure you either cover all the elements or go all-in on a specific type so you can streamroll bosses. While every attack chips at an enemy's stagger meter, hitting their weaknesses is, of course, the strategy demanded of you.

I'm of two minds with this system: while it’s nice to have flexibility as you swap Visions between party members to constantly change their overall movesets, it can sometimes trivialize your combat approach. For example, going into a water-themed boss fight, I knew purely electric builds were going to be the optimal strategy. So, while it was rad as hell to watch chunks of stagger and HP get chopped off as I spammed electric attacks, I often didn't feel the need to think much harder than that. Having the foresight to anticipate the right element before a fight isn't quite as rewarding as being pushed to scheme with what you have.

Compare this to the boost and break system of an Octopath Traveler, where the tools you're given are more dynamic and free-flowing even with elemental affinities involved, which then lets you get more creative rather than just having you hammer away with one specific element. I cruised through the first half of Resonance since most enemies and bosses were pushovers. But thankfully, things got tougher in the late game where they hit harder and inflicted more status ailments to work around. Key moments where I was challenged to think steps ahead culminated in some real hard-fought battles toward the end.

Overall, it still provides enough of the puzzle-esque tactical thinking that's required of a good turn-based RPG. Party members level up alongside their mastery of equipped Visions, but you have to manually rank up Visions then apply passive perks and support spells, which gets into some interesting buildcrafting that gives a little extra depth that mattered for those big fights. And I enjoyed Resonance's combat system because it still captures the satisfaction of teeing off on a staggered enemy with your nastiest spells, especially because their animations look so good and hit with emphatic impact.

Visions themselves are super fun to toy with because most of them are avatars of star characters from Final Fantasy's past. Their movesets call back to specific spells and signature attacks from their respective games, and it's nice to see parts of the series' history celebrated in a way that's integral to how Resonance plays. Staggering an enemy grants extra turns in a bonus phase, and staggering all of them (or a lone foe) leads to the sweeping stagger phase where everyone gets to pile on, which then concludes in a Resonance attack tied to a Vision of your choosing. I still find it jarring to go from beautiful HD-2D to a CGI cutscene (pulled from Brave Exvius) when summoning a Resonance attack, some of these are pretty cool, like big Shanttoto throwing a massive boulder of dark energy or Clive getting ready to hit L3+R3 to accept the truth. There's some wonderful pixel art around those cuts that look incredible, too, like Lightning, who gets a full animation set here – and it's lovely to see these characters recreated in that style.

Each is obtained by visiting shrines sprinkled throughout the overworld and going through a quiz-like dialogue sequence that walks through the events of their own stories (and beware, there are some major spoilers for Final Fantasies you have not played yet). I found this pretty cheesy at first, but it really grew on me as a reminder of how each entry captured something powerful that has stood the test of time. You never really know which shrine belongs to who, so when their music kicks in, it had me grinning ear-to-ear – and as someone who was deeply touched by FFXIV Shadowbringers, hearing "Tomorrow and Tomorrow" and recounting Y'shtola's ongoing story is a prime example of how sometimes Resonance got me.

More than the hard-fought battles against god-like beings, Final Fantasy has stuck around and won our hearts because of the stories it tells. And this is where I wrestled most with Resonance. The foundations of its story are quite solid and consistent as a classic Final Fantasy about the power of crystals that fuel these magical worlds and defeating evil to save the world against villains who reveal themselves to be more complicated by story's end. But it's always about how those stories get told and the impactful themes they explore along the way. Resonance has glimpses of hitting those same highs, yet I found long stretches of its storytelling to be quite underwhelming.

Taking the story of Brave Exvius and expanding on it was definitely worth exploring, but Resonance fills out a lot of that time with dialogue that feels like it was written for a middling young adult novel then crammed into a fantasy world. Not that fantasy stories need to be Shakespearean or high-concept, but much of Resonance reads like a script that didn't get punched up; overly talkative where it takes five lines for something that could've been said in one, and banking on a contemporary twee tone and some mustache-twirly villains. I love melodrama, long cutscenes, and tropes like the power of friendship, and Resonance has that for sure, but doesn't start dialing it in until late in the game.

"Octopath Traveler 0 asks you to stick with a 100-hour journey, and it rewards you with the kinds of moments only lengthy RPGs can pull off with its overarching story, an intricate turn-based combat system, and a soundtrack that'll leave you absolutely floored." - Michael Higham, December 19, 2025

But there's still something enticing about going on a journey with characters who overcome unbelievable odds. I came around on lead protagonist Rain and his brother-in-arms Lasswell because, while simple characters, they have a bond that riled me up for the conclusion. Fina turns out to be a little bit more than someone with a mysterious, dark past and was a compelling way to weave in more of the magical storytelling devices sensibly. The stern tactician Nichol and pink-haired mage Sakura turn out to be the better written characters who fit the RPG mold so well; and the emotional arc Nichol goes through is genuine and one of the few ways the story shows some depth. However, I struggled to care about the Sworn Six since a lot of their dialogue undersells their importance to the broader lore. And that Dr. Lazarov is an incredibly annoying throwaway who is nothing more than a mad scientist to roll your eyes at.

items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance: How To Get Y’shtola
items.summary: Y'shtola is a popular character from Final Fantasy XIV. She is also an obtainable Vision in Final Fantasy Resonance.
items.content:
Final Fantasy Resonance brings a lot of popular characters from the mainline Final Fantasy Series into the game as Visions. Visions can be equipped to your main characters to give them special abilities from the characters these Visions represent. In order to grab these Visions, you have to locate their Sanctums. Once you reach their Sanctum, you have to answer three questions. Regardless of your answers, you will receive the Vision. There are a lot of characters in Final Fantasy XIV . Y’shtola is one of the standouts of the bunch. She is a Vision you can receive in Final Fantasy Resonance .

As soon as you get the reveal of the location of the Fire Shrine in Final Fantasy Resonance , you will get a mission to go to the weapon factory. When you reach the Weapon Factory, do not go into it immediately. Instead, head southeast. The very next thing on the map southeast of the Weapon Factory will be the Sanctum of Y’shtola. Go to the Sanctum and add her to your party!

Y’shtola is a breaker unit who deals a good chunk of stagger damage with her magical spells. She deals Blizzard damage and Aero damage. She also has some nice support magic.

Final Fantasy Resonance will arrive on October 22nd, 2026, for PlayStation 5 , XBOX Series X|S , Nintendo Switch , Nintendo Switch 2 , and PC .

Final Fantasy 14 Accounts Suffer Major Data Breach
items.summary: Square Enix has stepped forward, requesting players reset their account information after a malicious third party obtains passwords.
items.content:
By Michael Manning Published Oct 19, 2026, 7:52 PM EDT Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of art has something worth celebrating. He's excited to bring this outlook to Dualshockers. Sign in to your DualShockers account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap The internet's constant presence in our lives makes juggling passwords a necessary evil, and many games and apps take the load off by storing these login methods. While this can be incredibly convenient, it also means that if any breaches occur, players are left to the wolves.

Despite the series constant presence in the gaming zeitgeist, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign brings enough new while respecting the old.

It's good practice to change your passwords on a regular basis, and Square Enix is asking Final Fantasy 14 players to do just that. In a blog post released just a few hours ago, the company revealed that a malicious third party has managed to breach player account information, and while they search for the culprits, all players are encouraged to reset their login credentials as soon as possible.

Data breaches are nothing new to the world of gaming, though the actual form varies from breach to breach. Some of the biggest i n the industry target developers themselves, either for company information or personal data, enabling leaks or straight-up fraud if the companies have enough personal information on their staff.

The other kind, afflicting Final Fantasy 14 players as we speak, is a player-targeted attack meant to steal personal data, likely for scams or to test these passwords on other platforms. This is just another reason to not reuse the same password on multiple accounts, as a single leak can compromise you across the internet.

This isn't the first account issue Final Fantasy 14 has had in the last year, with a mod back in 2025 revealing that Square tracks profiles between characters, allowing potential stalkers to follow victims through their alternates. This was quickly rectified after outrage, but sparked a discussion about how easy Square made it to keep an eye on other players' accounts, minimizing privacy.

Larger industry sentiments on data breaches have shifted slightly due to the ever-present nature of leaks, especially surrounding hotly anticipated titles. Players as a whole have grown a bit more patient with the individuals who enact these leaks, with situations like this one providing an important reminder of how important account security is.

While this can be incredibly convenient, it also means that if any breaches occur, players are left to the wolves.

To that end, Square is attempting to stave off the effects of the data breach by locking the accounts of players they believe are affected. These accounts will have emails sent to their primary addresses, allowing them to reset their account info immediately. Meanwhile, Square encourages the use of One-Time Passwords, a system that sends players a unique code every time they log in.

This way, even with your info leaked, you can ensure no one can log in to your account without your input, and you'll be alerted via the one-time password if someone is attempting to breach your account.

As the tools used to enact these breaches improve, it feels like the self-preservation of players has been steadily declining. Even as tools for multi-factor authentication get more and more trustworthy, players rely on in-app storage more than ever, allowing these breaches to land on target.

If the Sony and Nintendo data breaches taught us anything, it's that individual account security needs to become a larger priority both for players themselves and the developers who store our data. Square Enix still doesn't have a lead on who committed this particular breach, but previous incidents like this have involved individuals and groups alike.

Whether they intend to just sell the data off, hold it for ransom, or to let the breach itself sit as some kind of threat itself, Square Enix will need to step up the plate to regain player trust, especially with a new expansion right around the corner. Now isn't the time to lose players, right when the MMO winter season is ready to blow in.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV’s latest patch basically starts Evercold, but only gives you a short taste
items.content:
I know I said last time we’ve officially entered Evercold, but you can take that statement even more literally with patch 7.56. The MSQ for this patch is short but sweet, taking the Warrior of Light, Alphinaud, and Estinien to the fourth. There, we’re trapped on a deserted island, attacked by some strange machines, and saved by what is no doubt a teaser for the new ranged job to be revealed at the Tokyo Fan Fest. I won’t spoil it here, but it looks cool even if it isn’t exactly what I wanted. (I wanted something using Vanille’s whip staff thing from FFXIII, but maybe next time.) There’s unfortunately no dungeon or trial this time around, just two instanced battles, but both are a good time and interesting enough to engage you. The outfit you get at the end of the MSQ this time is also fantastic, and I’ve been using it as my Beastmaster outfit.

The focus of my time with this patch instead has been squarely on Beastmaster, the new Limited Job. As one of the few who love playing Blue Mage, I was stoked to have something similar again, and it seems a lot more people are enjoying this new job than did Blue Mage. That’s for good reason, as Beastmaster seems to focus way more on solo, open-world content instead of needing to go through party finder to get a group together for a dungeon. There is still some of that here, but most of the monsters you can tame are out in Eorzea.

More than anything, it’s nice to have something to do in these old zones again. I’ve been hunting down monsters to add to my besti-beastiery, fighting random mobs for experience, and running FATEs with other random players. That part alone is a lot of fun, but Beastmaster has its own unique gameplay style unlike any other job, even back when Summoner was actually a pet class. The basic loop for Beastmaster has you summon one of your three chosen monsters, then you and your companion attack an enemy to build up your respective TP bars. Once one of you reaches 100 TP, you can use a special color-coded attack, which will then reset your TP back to 0. Every monster only has one color attack, while you have all four at your disposal. To do some real damage, you need to follow up the first attack with the next in the sequence, shown going clockwise on your job gauge. So if you do a green move, your monster needs to use red, for example. Either one of you can start or end the combo too, but you still need to go in clockwise order to gain any bonus effects.

You’re not just waiting around to build up these combos, as there’s still a lot to consider in the moment-to-moment combat, even if it is overall slower-paced than the typical jobs in the game. When summoning a monster to the field, you gain the One with Nature buff, which allows you to use either Borrow or Tempered Release. Borrow lets you gain a special action based on the monster’s species for the duration they are on the field, while Tempered Release has your monster perform their unique skill. You can only use one per summon, so you need to choose wisely. You might want to borrow a cool dodge move that also grants you evasion up for a bit to dodge some incoming AoEs, or you might want your monster’s special healing skill for some more survivability overall. It’s a cool system even if it’s difficult to keep track of all the moving parts.

That difficult to keep track of theme continues in Beastmaster’s special solo content, the Crucible of the Unbroken. This is something of a rogue-like mode, where you move between spaces on a board game, with each space representing an encounter. You can pick a number of Beasties to join you on a board, but again, only three per battle, and all HP persists between encounters. You need to consider what monsters in your party will do the most damage or be the most survivable, when to use special items that grant healing, revives, or special buffs, and what temporary equipment you want to equip. It’s kind of a lot, but having only gone through the first board so far, it's a lot of fun too.

Overall, I’ve been having a blast with Beastmaster. While it can be a bit tedious to level at times, I’d prefer this be something that lasts me a good long while rather than speeding to the current cap of level 50. This’ll probably hold me over until Evercold at least, which is great because I just got all my other jobs to cap after my raiding group disbanded amicably, and I need things to do. Hope you enjoyed the read, and I’ll see you again next patch.

items.content:
It gives us great pleasure to announce the return of the Moogle Treasure Trove starting Wednesday, September 9, 2026! This Moogle Treasure Trove will be a special edition to celebrate the upcoming release of Evercold, taking part across two installments and with an even more exciting range of items, including a special reward: an uolon horn! As well as bestowing irregular tomestones as usual, the First Hunt for Astronomy will also reward those who complete minimog and ultimog challenges with a unique item required to obtain the uolon horn. Details can be found on the special site below. The First Hunt for Astronomy and the Second Hunt for Astronomy, to be held at a later date, will feature a different lineup of items and different tomestones required for exchange. However, please note that the uolon horn will be available in the Second Hunt as well. * Irregular tomestones of astronomy I will not be awarded when using adventurer squadrons or the Duty Support system. * Unrestricted parties must have the “Level Sync” option enabled to receive irregular tomestones of astronomy I.

Event Duration

From Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. (PDT) / 8:00 (GMT) / 9:00 (BST) / 18:00 (AEST) to Monday, October 19, 2026 at 7:59 a.m. (PDT) / 14:59 (GMT) / 15:59 (BST) / Tuesday, 20 October at 1:59 (AEDT) * Dates and times are subject to change. * Please note that it may take up to 10 minutes after the stated time for the event to commence in-game.

Rewards

Visit the special site for details.
